summary: This section explains how a company can issue securities to a select group of people through a private placement instead of a public offer. It sets strict rules on who can be offered shares, how money must be paid, and when shares must be allotted. If a company offers shares to too many people, the offer is treated as a public offer.
points: A company can make a private placement of securities only to a select group of identified persons whose number generally shall not exceed fifty in a financial year.
The private placement offer and application cannot carry any right of renunciation.
Subscribers must pay the subscription money using a banking channel like a cheque or demand draft, and not in cash.
A company must keep application money in a separate bank account and cannot use it until allotment and the return of allotment are filed.
Securities must be allotted within sixty days from the date of receiving the application money.
example: Meera Textiles Private Limited decided to raise funds by issuing shares through a private placement. The Board of Directors prepared a list of ten identified persons and sent them a private placement offer-cum-application. Mr. Roy, one of the identified persons, wanted to invest and paid his subscription money using a demand draft. Meera Textiles kept this money in a separate scheduled bank account. Within the required time, the company allotted the shares and filed a return of allotment with the Registrar, containing a complete list of all allottees.

terms.meaning: An offer or invitation to subscribe to securities given to a select group of persons rather than the general public.
The right to give up or pass on an offer to someone else.
The process of giving or distributing shares or securities to applicants.

watch: Exceeding the permitted number of persons makes the private placement legally treated as an offer to the public.
